newsitem.title: UK: Scientists find key to how immune system works.
newsitem.headline: Scientists find key to how immune system works.

text.p: Scientists said on Wednesday they had taken a big step forward in understanding how the immune system works by modelling how T-cells decide which cells are infected by a virus.
T-cells are the front-line of the body's defences, patrolling through the body, hooking up to other cells and checking to see if they are all right.

Scientists know that delicate chemical signalling is involved, but Don Garboczi, Don Wiley and colleagues at Harvard University's Howard Hughes Medical Institute reported in the science journal Nature they had tracked the molecular structure.
Most cells in the body carry a small molecule known as a peptide, which signals their condition.
"It's like a little flag that tells what's going on inside the cell. It could be "don't kill me I'm one of yours' or it could be 'danger -- kill'," Garboczi said in a telephone interview.
If a virus has infected the cell, the peptide will carry fragments of the virus and tip off the T-cell, which then destroys both the cell and its viral hijacker.

Garboczi's group used x-ray crystallography to examine the molecules involved. "We crystallised the whole complex, passed x-rays through the crystal and then anaylsed what the molecule looks like," he said.
The research, which took a year, involved a T-cell receptor specific to the human T cell lymphotropic virus (HTLV), which can cause some forms of leukaemia, Garboczi, a biochemist, said.
"This is a picture of just one T-cell receptor. They are like antibodies -- there are millions of them," he said.
Why HTLV? "This is the one that worked first," he explained. He said his group would now look at the structures involving T-cells that attack other viruses.
In a second study, Roy Mariuzza and colleagues at the University of Maryland's Biotechnology Institute discovered why some T-cells take things a bit too far.

T-cells can send out chemical signals calling other T-cells to a site. The idea is for them to work together to fight an infection, but sometimes they overdo it, as in toxic shock syndrome, some types of diabetes and multiple sclerosis.
They are prompted into this over-zealous effort by super-antigens, bits of bacterial or viral proteins that act like the peptides.
Mariuzza's group modelled these and found out how they bind to the T-cell. The way it does so bypasses normal processes, such as those described by Garboczi's group.
